entries.title: How did Benjamin Franklin help people share books and ideas?
entries.answer: Benjamin Franklin worked as a printer in Philadelphia before he became a famous public figure. Printing helped him share news and ideas with readers. He and a group of other people agreed to put money together to buy books for a library. Members could use more books together than they could each buy alone. Franklin later helped work on the Declaration of Independence and the United States Constitution. Finding practical ways for people to cooperate was one part of his long career.
facts: The Library Company of Philadelphia began in 1731.

entries.title: How did Frederick Douglass use speeches and writing to change minds?
entries.answer: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became a writer and public speaker. He described his own experiences so readers could understand how slavery harmed people and took away their choices. He also published a newspaper called The North Star. Newspapers and meetings let him reach people who had never heard him speak in person. He kept arguing for equality after slavery ended, because a constitutional change alone could not make neighbors or leaders treat people fairly.
facts: Douglass published the first of his autobiographies in 1845.

questions.text: What kinds of choices did people face when seeking freedom?

entries.title: How did Harriet Tubman help people reach freedom?
entries.answer: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland. She then returned many times to help family members and other people escape, using connections along the Underground Railroad. The trips could be dangerous, and she had to decide when to move and when to wait. She led dozens of people to freedom. During the Civil War she also helped the United States Army. Later, she used her experience and public voice to support equal rights, including women’s right to vote.
facts: Tubman made about thirteen trips back to Maryland to guide freedom seekers.

entries.title: How did Ida B. Wells use facts to fight injustice?
entries.answer: Ida B. Wells was a teacher and journalist. She investigated racist violence at a time when many newspapers gave reasons for attacks without checking them. She collected evidence that challenged what those papers said, then spoke and published what she had found. Wells also pressed for women’s voting rights. Her work could put her in danger, but it showed why asking careful questions and checking facts matter. Readers could use her research to challenge a story they had heard many times.
facts: Ida B. Wells helped organize a voting-rights club for Black women in Chicago.

entries.title: How did people build homes inside cliffs at Mesa Verde?
entries.answer: Ancestral Pueblo people farmed and lived in the Mesa Verde region of what is now Colorado. Some later homes were tucked under wide shelves in sandstone cliffs. Builders set stone walls behind the cliff edge, where parts of the rock made a natural roof. They found ways to reach different rooms with paths and ladders. People lived in several kinds of homes in the region, and the cliff dwellings came late in a much longer period of community life.
facts: Cliff Palace is one of the largest surviving cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde.

questions.text: How did Indigenous builders use soil to reshape another site?
How did people in the Andes also build around steep ground?
How can rock wear away to make a natural shelter?

entries.title: How did people keep a bus boycott going for more than a year?
entries.answer: Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, organized a boycott of the city buses in 1955 after Rosa Parks’s arrest. Many people walked, shared rides, or used carpools to keep going to work and school. Organizers gave rides, passed messages, and held meetings. The boycott lasted more than a year. Meanwhile, a court case brought by several Black women challenged the rules for buses. The boycott ended after a court ruling against bus segregation took effect.
facts: The boycott started in December 1955 and ended in December 1956.

entries.title: How did Sacagawea help the Lewis and Clark expedition?
entries.answer: Sacagawea traveled with the group led by Lewis and Clark while carrying her young child. She could speak languages that helped the explorers communicate. When the party needed horses to cross the mountains, it met a Shoshone group led by her brother. Her language skills helped with that meeting. She also helped in other ways on the long journey, though the expedition’s journals record only a small share of her life. Tribal histories preserve different details about her story.
facts: Written sources spell Sacagawea’s name in several different ways.

entries.title: How did the Erie Canal move boats across New York?
entries.answer: Before railroads reached many places, the Erie Canal let boats carry goods between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. Crews dug long channels and built gates that could close off a section. Workers filled or emptied the section to lift or lower a boat between different water levels. Such a section is called a lock. The canal made heavy loads easier and cheaper to move between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic coast, and towns along its route gained new trade.
facts: The Erie Canal opened in 1825.

entries.title: How did the Nineteenth Amendment change voting?
entries.answer: The Nineteenth Amendment says that a U.S. citizen’s right to vote cannot be denied because of their sex. In the years before 1920, some states already allowed women to vote in some or all elections, while others did not. After years of organizing and debate, enough states approved the amendment in 1920 for it to take effect across the country. People still faced other unfair barriers to voting. For instance, officials in some states continued to use racist rules and practices to turn Black citizens away.

sections.heading: A word for the right to vote
sections.text: Suffrage means the right to vote in political elections. People who worked for women’s suffrage organized meetings, wrote to leaders, and marched.

facts: Tennessee was the state whose approval in 1920 brought the amendment to the number required.
An amendment is an official change or addition to the Constitution.

entries.title: How did thirteen colonies become a new country?
entries.answer: The thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast included people who disagreed about who should make laws and collect taxes. Protest turned into fighting in 1775. In 1776, colonial leaders announced that the colonies were forming independent states. Their forces fought Britain, and France later helped them. Some people in the colonies supported Britain, and other communities faced choices and losses of their own. A peace treaty in 1783 recognized the United States as an independent country.
facts: The fighting lasted for several years after the Declaration of Independence.

Where did some of the first fighting happen?

entries.title: How did workers connect rail lines across the United States?
entries.answer: In the 1860s, the Central Pacific built tracks east from California while the Union Pacific built west from the middle of the country. Workers cut paths, moved earth, laid rails, and carried heavy equipment across mountains and plains. Many Chinese workers helped build the line from the west. The two companies joined their tracks in Utah in 1869. Long rail trips became easier, but building and expanding the rail network also brought changes and losses to Indigenous communities along the routes.
facts: The joining ceremony took place at Promontory Summit in Utah.

entries.title: What did Abigail Adams ask lawmakers to remember?
entries.answer: Abigail Adams wrote letters to her husband John while he worked with other leaders of the American Revolution. In March 1776 she expected new rules to be written and asked him to consider women’s rights in those rules. The letter lets us hear one person pointing out that demands for freedom could mean different things to different people. She had no vote at the meetings. Letters like hers survived, giving readers a record beyond speeches made by officials.
facts: Abigail wrote the letter before the colonies declared independence.

entries.title: What did George Washington do before and after independence?
entries.answer: George Washington was chosen to lead the Continental Army during the American Revolution. After the war, he led meetings at the Philadelphia convention that produced the United States Constitution. In 1789 he became the first president under the new Constitution. Many decisions about what a president does were still being worked out. When he left after two terms, another president could take office. Washington also held people in slavery on his Virginia estate, part of a wider contradiction in the new nation.
facts: George Washington served as president from 1789 to 1797.

entries.title: What did people ask for at the Seneca Falls convention?
entries.answer: In 1848 a group gathered in Seneca Falls, New York, to talk about women’s rights. Organizers used language from the Declaration of Independence in a new statement. They argued that women should have more rights in public life and under the law. The request for the right to vote drew disagreement, even among some people at the meeting. The convention mattered because it gave public form to demands that people continued to argue for over many decades.
facts: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott were among the convention’s organizers.

entries.title: What did the Declaration of Independence say?
entries.answer: In 1776, the Continental Congress approved a document saying that 13 British colonies in North America were separating from Great Britain. The Declaration of Independence explained why they were taking that step and described rights they said people should have. The war with Britain was already underway. The ideas in the document went farther than what the new country put into practice at the time. For example, slavery continued even after the leaders said that people were equal.

sections.heading: Two dates
sections.text: Congress adopted the text on July 4, 1776. Delegates began signing the large copy now at the National Archives on August 2. Some signed later.

facts: The document announced independence before the Revolutionary War ended.
The Declaration is preserved at the National Archives.

entries.title: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
entries.answer: President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, during the Civil War. It declared enslaved people free in places it listed as still in rebellion against the United States. It did not immediately free all enslaved people everywhere. Freedom in many places still depended on the United States Army gaining control. The order also allowed Black men to enter United States military service. The Thirteenth Amendment later ended slavery under the Constitution, with a narrow exception in the text.
facts: The official document listed which states or parts of states it applied to.

entries.title: What did the Lewis and Clark expedition set out to learn?
entries.answer: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led a group west in 1804. They traveled through country known to many Indigenous nations and kept notes about rivers, plants, animals, and people they met. They followed the Missouri River for part of the journey, crossed the mountains, and reached the Pacific Ocean. The travelers depended on directions, trade, and local knowledge. Journals from the journey record what members of the group saw, even though those accounts cannot represent everyone’s experience of the trip.
facts: The expedition returned to St. Louis in 1806, about two years after setting out.

entries.title: What did the United States try to rebuild after the Civil War?
entries.answer: Reconstruction was the period when the United States tried to reunite after the Civil War and decide how freedom would work in daily life. New constitutional amendments ended slavery, defined citizenship, and addressed racial barriers to voting. Black families built schools, searched for relatives, voted where allowed, and took part in public office. Many white leaders and groups resisted these changes. After federal protection weakened, state and local rules took away rights people had fought to use.
facts: The era is commonly dated from 1865 through 1877.

entries.title: What happened at Lexington and Concord?
entries.answer: On April 19, 1775, British soldiers marched from Boston toward Concord to seize supplies the colonists had stored. Local people spread the warning. In Lexington, colonists and soldiers faced one another, and shots were fired. Nobody can say for sure who fired the first shot. Fighting also broke out at Concord’s North Bridge. More colonists joined as British soldiers returned to Boston. These encounters turned a tense political dispute into open fighting in Massachusetts.
facts: The North Bridge site is part of Minute Man National Historical Park.

questions.text: How did the fighting grow beyond Massachusetts?

entries.title: What happened when travelers arrived at Ellis Island?
entries.answer: Ellis Island was a large United States immigration station in New York Harbor. Some travelers arriving by ship went there to have their papers checked and answer questions. Doctors also looked for health problems that could affect whether a person was allowed to enter under the rules of the time. Families might wait together or be separated during checks. Millions went through the station before it closed. Their arrival records help some families find out how their relatives came to the United States.
facts: The main immigration station opened in 1892.

entries.title: What was the city at Cahokia Mounds like?
entries.answer: Cahokia was a large Indigenous city near the Mississippi River, in what is now Illinois. Its people carried loads of soil to make raised mounds. Open spaces between some mounds gave people room to meet. Around these spaces were homes and areas for work. From the top of the largest mound, you could see far beyond the main plaza. Archaeologists study changes in the layout to learn how the city grew and how different spaces may have been used.
facts: Monks Mound is the biggest surviving mound at Cahokia.

entries.title: What was the Louisiana Purchase?
entries.answer: In 1803, the United States bought France’s claim to a large stretch of land west of the Mississippi River. American leaders wanted a reliable place to send goods through New Orleans, a busy port near the river’s mouth. The French offered a much larger deal. It made the area claimed by the United States nearly twice as large. Many Indigenous nations already lived there and had their own governments. A treaty between the United States and France did not mean those nations had agreed to give up their land.
facts: The Louisiana Purchase cost the United States about fifteen million dollars at the time.

entries.title: What was the Underground Railroad?
entries.answer: The Underground Railroad was a loose network of people, routes, and hiding places that helped enslaved people seeking freedom. Some people left on their own and received help along the way. Others knew someone who could offer a night’s shelter, information, food, or a ride. Freedom seekers made difficult choices about where to go and whom to trust. Journeys followed different routes and could go to Canada, Mexico, cities, or other communities. Its name compares the network to a railroad.
facts: Freedom seekers shaped and led many escapes with little or no help from an organized network.

entries.title: Why did delegates meet in Philadelphia in 1787?
entries.answer: After independence, the United States had a national government with limited power. Representatives met in Philadelphia in 1787 to consider changes. The delegates disagreed about how power should be split and how states would be represented. They also made compromises that protected slavery. The meeting produced an entirely new Constitution. The document proposed three branches of government and rules for approval by the states. Writing the plan at the convention was only one step toward putting it into use.
facts: Representatives from twelve of the thirteen states attended the convention.

How did writers try to persuade readers to approve it?
What responsibilities were put in three different branches?

entries.title: Why did Lincoln give a short speech at Gettysburg?
entries.answer: In November 1863, people gathered in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, to open a cemetery for soldiers who had fought there. After a long speech by another speaker, President Abraham Lincoln spoke briefly. He asked listeners to remember why the country had been founded and to continue the work of keeping a government chosen by its people. His speech linked the sacrifices of the war to the promise of equality. It is still studied for saying so much in only a few paragraphs.
facts: The speech came a few months after the Battle of Gettysburg.

entries.title: Why did protesters dump tea into Boston Harbor?
entries.answer: In 1773, Britain gave one company new ways to sell tea in its American colonies. A tax on the tea still applied. Some colonists thought buying it would mean accepting Parliament’s right to tax them without a voice there. In Boston, protesters boarded ships and threw chests of tea into the harbor. British leaders responded with laws that placed new restrictions on Massachusetts and closed the port to most trade for a time. The protest and response deepened the conflict.
facts: The Boston Tea Party happened the night of December 16, 1773.

How do elected representatives take part in making laws today?

entries.title: Why did the Supreme Court rule against separate public schools?
entries.answer: In several places, families challenged rules that sent Black and white children to separate public schools. The Supreme Court considered the cases together under the name Brown v. Board of Education. In 1954 it ruled that separating students by race in public schools broke the Constitution’s promise of equal protection. Changing schools took much more than one decision. Some places resisted, while children, families, teachers, and others kept working to make the ruling change real classrooms.
facts: The case was decided unanimously by the Supreme Court.

entries.title: Why did the United States fight a Civil War?
entries.answer: In 1861, a group of Southern states tried to leave the United States and formed the Confederacy. Their leaders wanted to protect slavery, a system that kept people forced to work as property. The United States government refused to accept the breakaway. Fighting began and lasted four years. During the war, ending slavery became a stated aim of the United States government. When the Confederacy surrendered, the country faced the work of rebuilding and of protecting the rights of people who had been enslaved.
facts: Most fighting ended in 1865.

entries.title: Why is Cherokee removal remembered as the Trail of Tears?
entries.answer: In the late 1830s, the United States government forced most Cherokee people in the southeastern United States to leave their homes. Soldiers gathered families, and groups traveled to lands far to the west. They took different routes by road and river. Cold, illness, and shortages harmed many travelers, and people died on the journeys and in camps. The name Trail of Tears helps people remember what happened, and Cherokee communities still tell the stories of families who were made to leave.
facts: A national historic trail follows several of the removal routes.

entries.title: Why was Rosa Parks’s bus ride important?
entries.answer: Rosa Parks had worked for civil rights for years before she was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955. On a city bus, a driver told her to give up her seat under rules that separated riders by race. She stayed seated. Local organizers then called for Black residents to stop taking the buses. People made different ways to get to work and school, and a court case challenged the rules. The bus ride mattered because many people were ready to act together.
facts: Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955.

entries.title: Why was Yellowstone made a national park?
entries.answer: Yellowstone became a national park in 1872. An important reason was that people wanted to keep its geysers, hot springs, and other unusual natural features protected and open to visitors. A geyser can send a burst of steam and water up from the ground. One famous geyser, Old Faithful, has drawn visitors for many years. Yellowstone also includes rivers, forests, and habitat for wildlife. Most of the park is in Wyoming, with parts in Montana and Idaho.

sections.heading: How to look
sections.text: At Yellowstone’s hot areas, visitors stay on boardwalks and other marked paths. Even ground that looks solid can be hot and unsafe.

facts: Yellowstone opened as the first U.S. national park.
It was set aside by a law passed by Congress and signed in 1872.
